## order-id.ts (core)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern branded-type
 * @options b5f8bd0193be398e
 */

/**
 * The mark that makes the type nominal.
 *
 * A `unique symbol` rather than the string tag this technique is usually shown
 * with. Two tags declared independently with the same text are structurally the
 * same type, so two modules that both reach for `"Id"` produce identifiers that
 * interchange with no diagnostic anywhere — where two symbols cannot collide
 * however their labels read.
 *
 * `declare` means no value is emitted. The mark exists for the compiler and
 * costs nothing at run time, which is the point: the value stays exactly the
 * primitive it was.
 */
declare const brand: unique symbol;

/**
 * An identifier that cannot be confused with any other string.
 *
 * An intersection, so `OrderId` is still accepted wherever `string` is —
 * `String.prototype` methods, a `Map` key, a template literal — while the
 * reverse is refused. That asymmetry is the whole pattern: it costs nothing at
 * the places a plain string already works, and it costs a compile error exactly
 * where a mistake was being made.
 */
export type OrderId = string & { readonly [brand]: "OrderId" };

/**
 * Marks a string without checking it.
 *
 * The only way in, deliberately. There is no rule to apply here: this rendering
 * is for values already valid by construction somewhere else — a key read back
 * from the store that wrote it — and a rule invented at this boundary would be
 * theatre that fails valid input.
 *
 * The name is the safeguard. This is the one hole in the guarantee, and it is
 * spelled so that it cannot be used by accident and cannot be read past in
 * review — where a helper called `toOrderId` would be reached for by everyone
 * and would quietly turn the type back into a `string`.
 */
export function unsafeOrderId(value: string): OrderId {
  return value as OrderId;
}
```

## order-id-example.ts (example)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern branded-type
 * @options b5f8bd0193be398e
 */

/**
 * Using the type, and the mistakes it refuses.
 *
 * The second half of this file is a set of assertions rather than a
 * demonstration. Each `@ts-expect-error` states that the line beneath it must
 * *not* compile, so if the guarantee ever lapsed the directive would go unused
 * and this file would stop compiling on that instead. It lives here rather than
 * in the test suite because the suite is optional and the guarantee is not.
 */

import { unsafeOrderId } from "./order-id.js";
import type { OrderId } from "./order-id.js";

/**
 * A second brand, for the mistake that matters most.
 *
 * Two arguments of the same primitive in the same signature is the shape of
 * every id-swap bug: nothing about `lookup(customer, order)` reads as wrong,
 * the arguments are the same type, and the test fixture that would catch it
 * uses the same value for both.
 */
declare const other: unique symbol;

export type CustomerId = string & { readonly [other]: "CustomerId" };

/**
 * Work that takes two identifiers of different kinds.
 *
 * The signature is now impossible to call wrongly. Unbranded, swapping the two
 * arguments compiles, runs, and returns a plausible URL for the wrong resource
 * — the class of bug that reaches production because every layer it passes
 * through agrees the types are fine.
 */
export function lookup(customer: CustomerId, order: OrderId): string {
  // Both are still strings, so every string operation is available unchanged.
  return `/customers/${customer}/orders/${order.toLowerCase()}`;
}

/**
 * The escape hatch, at the boundary it exists for.
 *
 * A row the store wrote is valid because something checked it before it went
 * in, which is the only claim this rendering makes.
 */
export function fromStore(row: { readonly id: string }): OrderId {
  return unsafeOrderId(row.id);
}

/**
 * The refusals, asserted.
 *
 * Everything below must fail to compile. `@ts-expect-error` inverts the usual
 * reading: it is satisfied by an error and violated by silence, so these lines
 * fail loudly if the type ever stops doing its job.
 *
 * The directive sits alone on its line with the reason above it. Written as one
 * long comment it would be re-wrapped to the margin, and a directive only
 * governs the line it begins on.
 */

export function refusesARawString(): void {
  // A plain string carries no evidence that anyone checked it.
  // @ts-expect-error
  const bad: OrderId = "ORD-1";

  void bad;
}

export function refusesTheOtherBrand(value: OrderId): void {
  // Two brands over the same string are still two types.
  // @ts-expect-error
  const bad: CustomerId = value;

  void bad;
}

export function refusesConcatenation(value: OrderId): void {
  // A template literal produces a plain string, mark and all discarded.
  // @ts-expect-error
  const bad: OrderId = `${value}-retry`;

  void bad;
}
```

## order-id.test-d.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern branded-type
 * @options b5f8bd0193be398e
 */

/**
 * What the compiler is asked to prove.
 *
 * Nothing here runs, and nothing here should: this file's suffix keeps it out
 * of every runner while leaving it in front of the compiler, which is the only
 * thing that can check a claim about a type. A brand that had stopped working
 * would behave identically at run time to one that still did.
 *
 * No claim below concerns nullability. With `strictNullChecks` off, `undefined`
 * is assignable to everything, so such a claim would mean one thing for one
 * caller and the opposite for another — and an assertion whose meaning depends
 * on the reader's compiler options is not one.
 */

import type { OrderId } from "./order-id.js";

/**
 * Forces its argument to be `true`, and fails to compile when it is not.
 *
 * Each assertion below is written as a named alias rather than a bare one, so
 * that it reads as a stated claim about the code and cannot be mistaken for a
 * leftover.
 */
export type Expect<T extends true> = T;

/**
 * Whether two types are identical, rather than merely assignable in both
 * directions.
 *
 * The two-function form looks like a trick because it is one: it compares the
 * types in a position the compiler checks by identity instead of by
 * assignability. The obvious alternative — asking whether each extends the
 * other — answers a different question, and answers it wrongly in two common
 * cases. It reports `true` for `any` against anything at all, and it
 * distributes over unions, so a union compared against one of its own members
 * can come back true.
 */
export type Equal<X, Y> =
  (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends <T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2
    ? true
    : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is assignable to `Y`.
 *
 * Both sides are wrapped in a tuple to stop the union distribution a bare
 * conditional performs. Undistributed is the question that was meant: whether
 * the whole of `X` is acceptable as a `Y`, rather than whether each member of
 * it is on its own.
 */
export type Extends<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? true : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is rejected where a `Y` is wanted.
 *
 * The type-level counterpart to `@ts-expect-error`, and preferable wherever the
 * claim is about a relationship rather than about a particular line: a
 * directive suppresses whichever error occurs, so it can be satisfied by an
 * unrelated mistake on the same line, where this cannot.
 */
export type NotAssignable<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? false : true;

/**
 * A raw `string` is refused where `OrderId` is wanted, which is the entire
 * point.
 */
export type RawIsRefused = Expect<NotAssignable<string, OrderId>>;

/**
 * And the converse holds, so nothing that already accepted a `string` has to
 * change.
 */
export type BrandIsStillAString = Expect<Extends<OrderId, string>>;

/**
 * Two brands over the same primitive do not interchange.
 *
 * Stated with a locally declared second symbol, because this is the claim that
 * would silently become false if the mark were a string tag: two tags reading
 * `"OrderId"` and `"CustomerId"` are different, but two modules that both
 * reached for the same word would not be.
 */
declare const other: unique symbol;
type CustomerId = string & { readonly [other]: "CustomerId" };

export type BrandsDoNotMix = Expect<NotAssignable<OrderId, CustomerId>>;
```

## order-id.test.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern branded-type
 * @options b5f8bd0193be398e
 */

/**
 * What is left for a suite that runs.
 *
 * Not the guarantee — that is settled before this file executes, and
 * `order-id.test-d.ts` is where it is asserted. What remains is the complement,
 * and it is worth more than it sounds: that the mark is *erased*. A caller has
 * to know the value is still a plain string at run time, or the type would be a
 * cost in disguise — breaking equality, `Map` keys, or a trip through JSON.
 */

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

import { unsafeOrderId } from "./order-id.js";
import type { OrderId } from "./order-id.js";

describe("OrderId at run time", () => {
  it("is exactly the primitive it wraps", () => {
    // The annotation is half the assertion. A brand widens to its base with no
    // cast, which is what keeps the value usable in code that never heard of
    // the type — and it is also what lets the comparison below be written at
    // all, since `toBe` is typed against whatever it was given.
    const erased: string = unsafeOrderId("ORD-1");

    expect(typeof erased).toBe("string");
    expect(erased).toBe("ORD-1");
  });

  it("compares and keys like the primitive", () => {
    const first = unsafeOrderId("ORD-1");
    const again = unsafeOrderId("ORD-1");

    // Identity has to be unchanged, or the type would have broken every `Map`,
    // `Set` and `===` it touches — a run-time cost for a compile-time
    // guarantee, which is not the trade on offer.
    expect(first === again).toBe(true);

    const seen = new Map<OrderId, number>([[first, 1]]);
    expect(seen.get(again)).toBe(1);
    expect(seen.get(unsafeOrderId("ORD-2"))).toBe(undefined);
  });

  it("survives a trip through JSON unchanged", () => {
    const value = unsafeOrderId("ORD-1");
    const round = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ value })) as { value: string };

    // The value survives; the *evidence* does not. What comes back is a plain
    // string, which is why a boundary reading it has to go through the
    // constructor again rather than assert its way in.
    expect(round.value).toBe("ORD-1");
  });
});
```
